name: Upwork
description: Largest general freelance marketplace. Hourly and fixed-price contracts with escrow protection and time tracking. Since 1 May 2025 the freelancer service fee is a variable 0–15% per contract (most freelancers ~10%), locked at proposal; Connects cost $0.15 each to bid. Weekly payouts via direct deposit, PayPal, Payoneer or wire.

pros: Largest client pool and highest volume of any freelance marketplace
Hourly contracts have full payment protection via Work Diary time tracking
Variable 0–15% fee can be as low as 0% on some contracts
Multiple payout rails with free ACH and weekly cadence
cons: Connects ($0.15 each) make bidding a real cost, especially for beginners
Fee is opaque — set per contract at proposal and not negotiable
High competition keeps entry-level rates low
Account suspensions can be abrupt and appeal is slow
reviewData.reviewBody:
Upwork remains the default freelance marketplace by volume, but its fee model changed on 1 May 2025: the old 20/10/5% sliding scale was replaced by a variable 0–15% service fee attached to each contract and locked the moment you submit a proposal — most freelancers land around 10%. Bidding costs Connects at $0.15 each (10 free per month), so proposal strategy matters.

Payouts run weekly (typically Wednesdays) via ACH (free), PayPal, Payoneer or wire, with daily payout available to established accounts. Hourly contracts are protected by the Work Diary time-tracking escrow. The platform's weakness is competition and account-suspension risk, but for established freelancers it delivers the most consistent client flow.
reviewData.testNotes: Fee change (1 May 2025) and payout schedule verified 25 Sep 2026 against Upwork's legal fee agreement and multiple 2026 fee guides. No live account test performed.

name: Fiverr
description: Fixed-price gig marketplace for design, programming, video, writing and marketing. Flat 20% seller commission on all orders, extras and tips. 14-day clearing period (7 days for Level 2/Top Rated/Pro/Seller Plus). Payout via PayPal (free, $1 min), Payoneer/bank transfer ($1, $20 min) or Fiverr Revenue Card.

reviewData.reviewBody:
Fiverr is the inbound-order alternative to bidding marketplaces: sellers list fixed-price gigs and buyers come to them, with no per-proposal cost. The trade-off is a flat 20% commission on every order, gig extra and tip — the highest standard rate among the major platforms. Funds clear after 14 days for new and Level 1 sellers, dropping to 7 days for Level 2, Top Rated, Pro and Seller Plus accounts.

PayPal withdrawals are free with a $1 minimum; Payoneer-powered bank transfer costs $1 with a $20 minimum, and the Fiverr Revenue Card costs $1 (2-day) or $3 (2-hour). Buyers pay 5.5% plus a small-order fee on top. For productized, repeatable services with fast delivery, Fiverr's volume usually justifies the cut; for high-end custom work, Upwork or a vetted network keeps more.
reviewData.testNotes: Commission, clearing periods and withdrawal fees verified 25 Sep 2026 against Fiverr's official Payment Terms (updated Aug 2026) and 2026 fee guides. No live account test performed.

name: Freelancer.com
description: Bidding marketplace with 1,350+ categories and contests. Freelancer fee 10% or $5 minimum (whichever greater) on fixed-price, hourly and contest payments. Withdrawal minimum $50 (wire $500); PayPal/Skrill/Payoneer $1 fee, wire $25, local bank deposit free where available.

reviewData.reviewBody:
Freelancer.com is the volume-bidding marketplace: 10% or $5 (whichever is greater) on every fixed-price, hourly and contest payment, with milestone escrow for protection. The $5 floor is punishing on small jobs — a $10 task effectively costs 50%. Withdrawals require a $50 balance ($500 for wire), and PayPal/Skrill/Payoneer withdrawals cost $1 each, while international wire costs $25; local bank deposits are free where available.

The free plan is very limited (bids, features), so most active freelancers end up on a paid membership tier. For freelancers in regions with local-bank-deposit support and a steady flow of mid-size projects, it remains a viable secondary source; for everyone else, Upwork or Fiverr usually net more.
reviewData.testNotes: Fee structure and withdrawal minimums verified 25 Sep 2026 against Freelancer.com's official Fees & Charges page (updated Sep 2026). No live account test performed.

name: PeoplePerHour
description: UK-founded freelance marketplace with Hourlies (fixed-price offers) and custom projects. Sliding freelancer fee: 20% on first £500 per client, 7.5% £501–£3,000, 3.5% above £3,000. Escrow protection; UK bank/SEPA withdrawals free, PayPal 2%. Strong UK/EU presence.

reviewData.reviewBody:
PeoplePerHour is the UK/EU-focused marketplace combining fixed-price 'Hourlies' with custom projects, all protected by escrow. Its freelancer fee slides per client: 20% on the first £500, 7.5% from £501–£3,000, and 3.5% above £3,000 — so repeat relationships get materially cheaper. Clients pay a 10% + £0.60 deposit fee into escrow, and freelancers withdraw free via UK bank or SEPA (PayPal costs 2%).

A notable term: dormant balances held over 30 days can incur admin fees, so withdraw promptly. Volume is lower than Upwork/Fiverr and skews UK/EU, but for freelancers in those markets building repeat clients, the sliding 3.5% end-rate is among the best in marketplaces.
reviewData.testNotes: Sliding fee and withdrawal fees verified 25 Sep 2026 against PPH terms (updated Sep 2026) and 2026 fee comparisons. Thresholds vary slightly by source (£350/£5,000 vs £500/£3,000); £500/£3,000 is the most-cited current structure. No live account test.

Guru is the low-fee incumbent: its SafePay escrow system predates most competitors, and freelancer fees run 5–9% depending on membership tier — Basic (free) pays 9% with 120 bids/year, while paid tiers ($11.95–$49.95/month) drop the fee to 5% and increase bid allocation. Clients pay a 2.9% handling fee, fully refunded when paying by eCheck or wire.

Withdrawals run weekly but carry per-method fees: PayPal $0.50, Payoneer $1.50, wire $15. Project volume is lower than Upwork, so Guru works best as a secondary channel or for freelancers willing to pay for a membership tier that lowers the effective take.
reviewData.testNotes: Fee tiers and withdrawal fees verified 25 Sep 2026 against Guru's help center and 2026 fee comparisons. No live account test performed.

Clients pay a flat $2–$29 project fee; Contra Pro/Max subscriptions can waive payment-processing fees. Payout via Stripe to bank. Best for creatives and independents who bring their own clients.

reviewData.reviewBody:
Contra's pitch is simple and rare: 0% commission to freelancers, always. Instead, clients pay a flat $2–$29 project fee, and Contra Pro/Max subscriptions ($/month) can waive payment-processing fees entirely. Payouts run through Stripe to a bank account in 2–3 business days.

The trade-off is volume: Contra's inbound client flow is a fraction of Upwork's, and opportunity access varies by plan. It shines for freelancers who already have clients and want a polished, fee-free invoicing/escrow layer, or for creatives building a portfolio presence. As a sole source of clients, it's thinner than the marketplaces.
reviewData.testNotes: 0% commission and client-fee model verified 25 Sep 2026 against Contra's own payments blog (Feb 2026) and 2026 comparisons. Pro/Max pricing varies; confirm in dashboard. No live account test performed.

name: Toptal

Freelancers set their own rate and pay 0% platform fee; Toptal's margin is a client-side markup (~40–60%) plus a $79/mo client fee. Monthly invoicing, payout via wire or Payoneer. Trustpilot ~4.8/5.

reviewData.reviewBody:
Toptal is the elite end of freelance: a multi-stage screening accepts roughly 3% of applicants, and accepted talent set their own rate with 0% platform fee — Toptal's margin lives in a client-side markup of roughly 40–60% plus a $79/month client fee. Typical freelancer rates run $60–$150+/hour, higher for niche specialists, with enterprise clients including Fortune 500 companies.

Payout is monthly by invoice via wire or Payoneer — slower cash flow than weekly marketplaces, but engagements are long-term and high-value. The screening is long and selective, and the platform is limited to software, design, finance and project management. For senior specialists who pass, it's the highest-paying, lowest-hassle channel; for everyone else, the vetting itself is the barrier.
reviewData.testNotes: 0% freelancer fee, client markup and $79/mo client fee verified 25 Sep 2026 against Toptal talent FAQ and 2026 breakdowns. Acceptance rate (~3%) is Toptal's own long-standing claim. No live account test performed.

Malt is strong in France (its origin), Germany, Spain and the UK, focused on tech, data, consulting and creative professionals. Its weakness is reach outside Europe and a requirement for proper invoicing status. For EU-based professionals, the 0% fee and fast payout make it a primary channel; for US/Asia freelancers, the client base is too thin.

A key UK-specific benefit is that YunoJuno handles IR35 status determinations and contracts, removing a major administrative burden for limited-company contractors.

It is UK-only and curated rather than fully open self-service, and it skews toward longer contracts rather than one-off projects. For UK creative/tech contractors who get accepted, the combination of 0% fee, fast payout and IR35 handling is hard to beat.

reviewData.reviewBody:
Bark is a lead-generation platform, not a freelance marketplace: professionals buy credits (bundles from roughly £20, varying by category) to receive and respond to customer leads, and pay 0% commission on any work they win — clients pay professionals directly. It covers trades, tutoring, design, marketing, events and wellness across the UK, US, Australia and beyond.

The model's strength and weakness are the same: you pay for leads regardless of whether you win the job. For high-ticket services with good conversion, the effective cost per acquired client can be low; for price-sensitive categories, lead quality is often poor. There is no escrow or payment protection. Best treated as a marketing channel with a tracked cost-per-acquisition, not a guaranteed work source.

reviewData.reviewBody:
99designs (owned by Vista) is the design-specialist marketplace with two work routes: design contests (submit concepts, winner takes the funded prize) and 1-to-1 direct projects. On direct projects, designers pay a platform fee by level: 5% (Top), 10% (Mid) or 15% (Entry), plus a $100 introduction fee per new client, capped and spread over the first $500 billed. Contest prizes have the platform margin built in, so winners receive the advertised amount.

Payouts run via PayPal with a commonly cited ~$25 minimum. The model rewards designers who level up (Top pays just 5%), but contest work is speculative — most entries earn nothing. For dedicated designers it's the strongest design-specific channel; for generalists it's irrelevant.

Dribbble is a portfolio network and job board, not a transactional marketplace: it takes 0% commission on freelance work, earning instead from designer Pro subscriptions (~$5/month annual) and employer job-posting fees. Designers find freelance work through the job board and inbound client messages, and get paid directly by clients — Dribbble holds no funds and provides no escrow.

Its value is discovery and prestige: a strong Dribbble profile generates inbound leads that convert off-platform. The trade-off is no payment protection or invoicing infrastructure, and hiring skews toward full-time roles. For designers it's best treated as a top-of-funnel channel paired with direct invoicing (Stripe, PayPal, Contra).
